content:
To complete some discussion on github, I drafted cslib#1011 showing what an inductive definition of LTS.Evaluation would look like. I'll defer to the people (particularly @Ching-Tsun Chou) who have more stake in this part of the library as to whether this is welcome — the PR is just to provide something concrete to discuss.

Some things to note:

  • All that has changed is the defeq of Evaluation — the same constructor and projections are available, just not anonymously (with ⟨...⟩).
  • Personally I find the alternate proofs quite readable and idiomatic. For example, Execution.comp is now a five-line induction, instead of requiring a helper lemma & lots of grinds and simps.
  • Despite adding several new results, the number of instructions for ‎Cslib/Foundations/Semantics/LTS/Execution.lean has more than halved. (There are a couple of downstream files which took a little longer, i think because grind had to find the projections out of Execution where before they were deconstructed manually — this should be fixable.)

The reasons (as I understand it) to keep the def as-is would be a) it matches well with OmegaExecution, and b) potentially it matches paper presentations more closely, so might be easier to parse for a reader. The latter difficulty could probably be eased with the right documentation, and to me this is the kind of difference that is common when translating informal maths into type theory.

That's what I proposed once, but we decided against it for reasons I don't clearly recall. @Ching-Tsun Chou maybe you do?

IIRC it was because we didn't really need the inductive side of this, whereas you needed the extensional one in your proofs. But if we need both sides, then it's probably fine to have inductive as the base one and the extensional thing as an API.
I corrected the subject line. It was LTS.Evaluation.

@Thomas Waring How about we just add the induction theorem for LTS.Executionas you formulated in one of the comments in cslib#981?
https://github.com/leanprover/cslib/pull/981#pullrequestreview-5366426996
This way anyone who likes to think inductively can use that theorem and do induction.

I'm not sure your theorem LTS.Execution.mk is the equivalent of the current definition of LTS.Executon as a structure. First, it doesn't look as nice. Second, your new proofs of buchiCongruence_transfer and Execution.reverse do not seem to be improvements over the old proofs using the current definition. Third, I notice that you added #grind_lint skip Cslib.LTS.Execution.trans, while removing #grind_lint skip Cslib.LTS.Execution.refl. I'm pretty sure I can replace the grind in the latter with a more manual proof. Can you do so easily for the former using the inductive definition?

Also, notice that your inductive definition has a built-in bias: the recursion is at the front end of the execution. But often (for example, in automata theory) we want to do induction at the back end. So we either provide an API for that, or use a definition that is not biased toward either possibility. I prefer the latter option.

Finally, I really do not believe in your claim that:

b) potentially it matches paper presentations more closely, so might be easier to parse for a reader. The latter difficulty could probably be eased with the right documentation, and to me this is the kind of difference that is common when translating informal maths into type theory.

I think that reflects more the bias of computer science than what proofs one can do in type theory.

I'll respond to these points, but I'm not invested enough to argue here — I'm judging on the info I have, but you know the library better so if you disagree that's fine. Thanks for taking the time to look it over.

  • On LTS.Execution.mk: you're right that they the structure definition looks different but unless I'm severely misunderstanding that's cosmetic, my .mk is literally identical to what the structure gives you.
  • Those proofs had to be changed because there is no longer a grind annotation on Execution.mk. I've replaced the reverse one with what I feel to be an idiomatic inductive proof, and the buchiCongruence_transfer one is longer because it was taking a while to elaborate, not because it needed to be (in fact, the old proof works verbatim — you can even delete the call to → LTS.Execution.of_mTr in the grind).
  • I _believe_, though I might be wrong, that there already was (effectively) a grind annotation on LTS.Execution.trans, because the definition of LTS.Execution was tagged. Perhaps this is something that is missed by the grind_lint machinery? @Chris Henson probably understands this better.
  • That's a fair point about the bias in direction. Still, to me that's not hard to overcome (see new proof of reverse), and note that the old API is all still there.
  • I'm not sure I understand what you mean in the last point, sorry. Do you mean that inductive definitions are more used in mathlib because of a computer science bias?

Like I said it's your call, I'm not trying to mess up your hard work downstream :)
re performance, i played with the proof of buchiFamily_saturation a bit and now that file is at -25% against master.

As I suggested, why not just add the induction principle to enable inductive proofs on LTS.Execution? An induction principle that recurses at the tail end of an execution would also be nice. Then you (and anyone else) can fix ugly proofs as they see fit;

I can do that, this just seems cleaner and has identical API — currently I'm just trying to understand what the problem with the inductive definition is. (Also I was working on the basis that people find custom induction principles hard to read / use, as was mentioned in the github thread.)

For me the problem with custom inductive definition is that one has to (so to speak) start from scratch for each new inductive definition. I'd rather rely on the vast number of results that are already proved about Nat and List (not to mention decision procedures) in mathlib. I also find it hard to wrap my head around inductive proofs about custom inductive definitions, but that is no doubt due to my own deficiency.
BTW, an inductive principle for LTS.MTr that recurses on the right would be nice, too.

Ching-Tsun Chou said:

I also find it hard to wrap my head around inductive proofs about custom inductive definitions, but that is no doubt due to my own deficiency.

To me the exact opposite is true... at first glance I had no clue what the definition did until I looked at the inductive version that Thomas wrote. It's much more in line with how we work with relations in Lean. I'd rather have that definition and offer the current version as an alternate constructor. We can hopefully tweak the cosmetics as needed so it's not an annoying transition for what you're upstreaming.

Ching-Tsun Chou said:

Also, notice that your inductive definition has a built-in bias: the recursion is at the front end of the execution. But often (for example, in automata theory) we want to do induction at the back end. So we either provide an API for that, or use a definition that is not biased toward either possibility. I prefer the latter option.

It's just more standard (and much nicer to work with in my opinion) to add this as an additional induction principle. An analogous example is the reflexive transitive closure, which has docs#Relation.ReflTransGen.tail as a constuctor, but at any time you can choose to use docs#Relation.ReflTransGen.head and docs#Relation.ReflTransGen.head_induction_on instead.

I think you consider recursing on the left is "just more standard (and much nicer to work with in my opinion)" only because that's how List is defined in mathlib. In other words, your view of what is natural is influenced by what's in mathlib. Mathematically speaking, there is no reason why LTS.MTr or LTS.Execution must be defined by recursing on the left. In fact, most automata theory textbooks use recursion on the right in both definitions and proofs related to our notions of LTS.MTr and LTS.Execution .

I agree with this statement:

I'd rather have that definition and offer the current version as an alternate constructor.

Whether an individual proof is better suited by one representation or another is a matter of the particulars. Having both seems helpful and this direction is easiest.

@Ching-Tsun Chou You have misunderstood what I was referring to with "standard". I meant only a preference for an inductive type versus the current structure. It is an implementation detail which direction is provided as a constructor and which is provided as an alternative induction principle, which is what I was trying to demonstrate with the example I linked to. You can and should have access to both.

Indeed, I think it is a "yes, and" situation. I am not 100% sure of the changes of the proofs however, I think where we were better suited by the original representation we should translate and leave them how they were.

I have already stated my personal preference: leave the definition of LTS.Execution as it is and add induction principles. I don't see any compelling reason to change the current definition other than personal aesthetic preference.
I am definitely sympathetic to that, especially if it delays ongoing work by creating thrash.
The performance benefits are also not negligible here, -1.67% for the overall library and multiple files cut in half by instruction count.

Where does the performance benefit come from? @Thomas Waring mentioned the theorem buchiFamily_saturation above. But this theorem's proof doesn't do induction on LTS.Execution. So how does an inductive definition of LTS.Execution make any difference?

Well, it might make a difference it terms of the patterns that grind uses. As I recall, when that proof was added I had a heck of a time golfing it in the review, so I'm not surprised it's a little sensitive to this sort of thing.
In that case, perhaps the right thing to do is to exert more manual control what lemmas grind has available.

a chunk of the improvement is from my golfs to buchiFamily_saturation, which can be considered separately, you're right (there are changes of the form Chris mentions, eg in files I didn't touch) — however the change to the file LTS.Execution (-21G) is purely from the change to an inductive definition. i also haven't tried to propagate the inductive idiom to further files, so it's possible there are further genuinely improvements to be found.
What is the "21G"?

latest round of golfs to buchiFamily_saturation gives

... BuchiCongruence//instructions: -17.4G (-46.02%)

oops sorry that's a reduction in number of instructions, corresponding to reducing the build effort of that file by two thirds, from the radar report on the PR:

build/module/Cslib.Foundations.Semantics.LTS.Execution//instructions: -21.8G (-68.03%)
OK, that makes more sense. If you see a significant performance benefit, then it makes sense to change the definition.
FWIW, I think I tried this same refactor, and didn't have the motivation to finish it. I agree this looks like a great improvement.

Indeed @Ching-Tsun Chou is correct that you can get the same thing logically by defining a suitable recursion principle, but you miss out on support in match expressions, and perhaps also in dependent eliminators?

Here's another argument for why the inductive definition is better: I would claim it is easier to look at that definition and say "this definitely models what an execution is"; the index-based definition requires you to more carefully look for off-by-one or nat truncation errors

OK. But is there a good argument for defining LTS.Execution by recursing on the left end (as opposed to the right end) other than the fact that List is defined by recursing on the left end? This always bothers me because in automata theory textbook proofs the induction is typically on the right end.
If you want to go in this direction,you could perhaps argue the list of states should be reversed too

Thanks all, I will spent some time making this more complete / presentable and ping back here when I have something ready for review. As a start, I think the performance improvements to the Buchi congruence proofs are pretty independent, so I'll split them out to review first.

See cslib#1027 — i went a little further than in the draft PR from yesterday, adding some results which helped make proofs i find to be readable. Overall change is -1.31% for the library, and -54.32% and -45.31% for BuchiCongruence and OmegaExecution respectively.

Thanks for golfing buchiFamily_saturation, which is one of the hardest proofs I had to do. I have two thoughts about this:
(1) I suspect that a lot of the performance gain is obtained by replacing grind with more manually directed proofs. I would really be nice if grind can give us some hints about how to find such proofs.
(2) I wonder if there is a coinduction principle which can simplify reasoning about OmegaSequence.flatten. It is very painful to work with Nat.segment. But I couldn't figure out any other way to define OmegaSequence.flatten.

No worries! I can certainly see why, it took me a while to understand the proof (lean or otherwise) — hopefully the comments I added are helpful for anyone looking in future.

On (2) I had a similar thought, I’ll think more & see if I can come up with anything.

Here's one option, not sure it would be any better

import Cslib

namespace Cslib.ωSequence

open Filter

variable {α : Type*} {xs : ωSequence (List α)}

def Productive (xs : ωSequence (List α)) : Prop :=
  ∃ᶠ (n : ℕ) in atTop, 0 < (xs n).length

def Productive.idx (h : xs.Productive) : ℕ :=
  Nat.find <| frequently_atTop.mp h 0

lemma Productive.idx_spec (h : xs.Productive) : xs h.idx ≠ [] :=
  List.length_pos_iff.mp (Nat.find_spec <| frequently_atTop.mp h 0).2

lemma Productive.drop_iff (xs : ωSequence (List α)) (n : ℕ) :
    (xs.drop n).Productive ↔ xs.Productive := by
  simp_rw [Productive, get_drop,
    ← frequently_map (m := (n + ·)) (P := (fun m ↦ 0 < (xs m).length)),
    show (fun x ↦ n + x) = (fun x ↦ x + n) by grind, map_add_atTop_eq_nat n]

lemma Productive.tail_iff (xs : ωSequence (List α)) :
    xs.tail.Productive ↔ xs.Productive := by
  rw [tail_eq_drop, drop_iff xs 1]

def Productive.pop (h : xs.Productive) : α × ωSequence (List α) :=
  ((xs h.idx).head h.idx_spec, (xs h.idx).tail ::ω xs.drop (h.idx + 1))

lemma Productive.pop_right (h : xs.Productive) :
    h.pop.2.Productive := by
  rw [← tail_iff]
  simpa [pop, drop_iff]

def Productive.getNext : {xs : ωSequence (List α)} → xs.Productive → ℕ → α
  | _, h, 0 => h.pop.1
  | _, h, n + 1 => h.pop_right.getNext n

noncomputable def flatten' [Inhabited α] (xs : ωSequence (List α)) : ωSequence α where
  get :=
    have := Classical.propDecidable xs.Productive
    if h : xs.Productive then h.getNext else fun _ ↦ default

end Cslib.ωSequence

the generalisation to ∃ᶠ (n : ℕ) in atTop, 0 < (xs n).length could well be an unnecessary headache, but we could provide a transformation dropping all the nil lists and prove flatten is invariant under that. (Noting eg docs#Filter.extraction_of_frequently_atTop.)

some proof of concept below for posterity — the frequently generalisation does introduce a bit of cruft, but it makes the coinductive arguments easier since ((x :: l) ::ω xs).flatten' = x ::ω (l ::ω xs).flatten even when l is empty

rescued from the online editor

lemma Productive.tail (h : xs.Productive) : xs.tail.Productive :=
  (tail_iff xs).mpr h

lemma Productive.of_tail (h : xs.tail.Productive) : xs.Productive :=
  (tail_iff xs).mp h

lemma Productive.idx_of_eq_nil (h : xs.Productive) (h₀ : xs 0 = []) :
    h.idx = h.tail.idx + 1 := by
  have : ∃ n, 0 ≤ n + 1 ∧ 0 < (xs (n + 1)).length := by simpa using frequently_atTop.mp h.tail 0
  convert! Nat.find_comp_succ (frequently_atTop.mp h 0) this (by simpa)
  simp_rw [idx]
  congr
  simp

lemma Productive.idx_of_ne_nil (h : xs.Productive) (h₀ : xs 0 ≠ []) :
    h.idx = 0 := by
  simpa [idx, Nat.find_eq_zero, List.length_pos_iff]

lemma Productive.pop_of_eq_nil (h : xs.Productive) (h₀ : xs 0 = []) :
    h.pop = h.tail.pop := by grind [pop, h.idx_of_eq_nil h₀]

lemma Productive.pop_of_ne_nil (h : xs.Productive) (h₀ : xs 0 ≠ []) :
    h.pop = ((xs 0).head h₀, (xs 0).tail ::ω xs.tail) := by
  simp [pop, h.idx_of_ne_nil h₀, tail_eq_drop]

lemma Productive.getNext_zero_of_ne_nil (h : xs.Productive) (h₀ : xs 0 ≠ []) :
    h.getNext 0 = (xs 0).head h₀ := by
  simp [getNext, h.pop_of_ne_nil h₀]

lemma Productive.getNext_succ_of_ne_nil (h : xs.Productive) (h₀ : xs 0 ≠ []) (n : ℕ) :
    h.getNext (n + 1) = h.pop_right.getNext n := by simp [getNext, h.pop_of_ne_nil h₀]

lemma Productive.getNext_of_eq_nil (h : xs.Productive) (h₀ : xs 0 = []) :
    h.getNext = h.tail.getNext := by
  ext n
  cases n <;> simp [getNext, h.pop_of_eq_nil h₀]

lemma Productive.head_flatten'_of_ne_nil [Inhabited α] (h : xs.Productive) (h₀ : xs 0 ≠ []) :
    xs.flatten'.head = (xs 0).head h₀ := by
  simp [flatten', h, h.getNext_zero_of_ne_nil h₀]

lemma Productive.tail_flatten'_of_ne_nil [Inhabited α] (h : xs.Productive) (h₀ : xs 0 ≠ []) :
    xs.flatten'.tail = ((xs 0).tail ::ω xs.tail).flatten' := by
  ext n
  have h' : ((xs 0).tail ::ω xs.tail).Productive := .of_tail h.tail
  simp only [flatten', h, ↓reduceDIte, get_tail, get_fun, h']
  convert h.getNext_succ_of_ne_nil h₀ n
  simp [h.pop_of_ne_nil h₀]

lemma flatten'_cons_of_productive [Inhabited α] {l : List α} (h : xs.Productive) :
    (l ::ω xs).flatten' = l ++ω xs.flatten' := by
  have hcons : (l ::ω xs).Productive := .of_tail h
  induction l with
  | nil =>
    simpa [flatten', h, hcons] using hcons.getNext_of_eq_nil
  | cons x l ih =>
    rw [← ((x :: l) ::ω xs).flatten'.eta, cons_append_ωSequence]
    congr
    · simp [hcons.head_flatten'_of_ne_nil (by grind)]
    · have : (l ::ω xs).Productive := .of_tail h
      simpa [hcons.tail_flatten'_of_ne_nil (by grind)] using ih this

lemma flatten'_eq_of_productive [Inhabited α] (h : xs.Productive) :
    xs.flatten' = xs.head ++ω xs.tail.flatten' := by
  rw [← xs.eta]
  exact flatten'_cons_of_productive h.tail

we could even use:

lemma not_productive_iff : ¬ xs.Productive ↔ ∃ N, xs.drop N = .const [] := by
  simp only [Productive, not_frequently, not_lt, nonpos_iff_eq_zero, List.length_eq_zero_iff,
    eventually_atTop, const, ωSequence.ext_iff, drop, get_fun]
  congr! 2 with n
  grind [n.exists_eq_add_of_le]

noncomputable def trivIdx (h : ¬ xs.Productive) : ℕ :=
  (not_productive_iff.mp h).choose

noncomputable def flatten'' [Inhabited α] (xs : ωSequence (List α)) : ωSequence α :=
  have := Classical.propDecidable xs.Productive
  if h : xs.Productive then ⟨h.getNext⟩ else (xs.take (trivIdx h)).flatten ++ω const default

in which case xs.flatten'' = xs.head ++ω xs.tail.flatten'' is true unconditionally

I think the use of ωSequence.Productive is an overkill [*] and, more importantly, obscures the real difficulties of defining and reasoning about OmegaSequence.flatten. If we continue to assume that ∀ n, 0 < (xs n).length, does your definition above actually define OmegaSequence.flatten? I can't tell by reading it. Maybe things will become clearer if we stick to the old assumption that ∀ n, 0 < (xs n).length?

[*] In all the applications of OmegaSequence.flatten I've had, I never found it hard to satisfy the assumption that ∀ n, 0 < (xs n).length`.
Also, I think we can define Productive.flatten in terms of OmegaSequence.flatten using Nat.nth.

BTW, I asked Claude (Opus 5.5) how ωSequence.flatten should be defined. It made two suggestions, one of which is essentially the definition I used. But the other one is something I hadn't thought of:

/-- The concatenation of the first `n` blocks. -/
def prefixConcat (xls : ℕ → List X) (n : ℕ) : List X :=
  ((List.range n).map xls).flatten

lemma le_length_prefixConcat (xls : ℕ → List X) (h : ∀ n, 0 < (xls n).length) :
    ∀ m, m + 1 ≤ (prefixConcat xls (m + 1)).length := by
  intro m
  induction m with
  | zero => simpa [prefixConcat] using h 0
  | succ m ih =>
    have := h (m + 1)
    simp only [prefixConcat, List.range_succ, List.map_append, List.flatten_append,
      List.length_append] at ih ⊢
    simp
    omega

def concatAll (xls : ℕ → List X) (h : ∀ n, 0 < (xls n).length) : ℕ → X :=
  fun m => (prefixConcat xls (m + 1))[m]'(by
    have := le_length_prefixConcat xls h m; omega)

It is quite an ingenious idea. I don't know if it would simplify things.
Oh that's quite nice, & might play well with the api you've already developed for omega sequences

In any case, cslib#1011 is now ready for review, as is the basically trivial speedup pr #1028 :-)
